evidence.quote:
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

raw = np.load("features.npz")
X = raw["features"]
y = raw["labels"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

ds = TensorDataset(torch.tensor(X_train), torch.tensor(y_train))
train_loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

for features, labels in train_loader:
    outputs = model(features)
    loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

findings.message: Cell 3 calls loss.backward() and optimizer.step() on every batch but never resets gradients. PyTorch accumulates into .grad, so from the second batch on, Adam steps on the running sum of every gradient seen so far, each computed at older weights, instead of on the current batch's gradient. Adam's per-parameter normalisation keeps the step size bounded, but the step direction is dominated by stale history. Training runs without any error and silently follows the wrong update rule. Search boundary: all four cells of train.ipynb contain no zero_grad call (optimizer or model) and no .grad reset.
findings.suggestion: Call optimizer.zero_grad() at the top of the loop body, before outputs = model(features).
findings.title: Gradients are never zeroed, so each step uses the sum of all previous batch gradients

findings.message: scaler.fit_transform(X) runs on the full dataset, then train_test_split divides X_scaled. The mean and standard deviation applied to the training data therefore include the 20% test rows, and any evaluation on X_test could be optimistic. Trigger: this has no effect on the current notebook, which never reads X_test, but it becomes leakage as soon as a test evaluation is added. Search boundary: no other scaler fit or transform exists in the four cells.
findings.suggestion: Split X first, then call scaler.fit_transform(X_train) and scaler.transform(X_test).
findings.title: StandardScaler is fit on all rows before the train/test split

findings.message: torch.tensor(X_train) keeps the NumPy dtype. StandardScaler produces float64 unless the input is already float32, and nn.Linear weights are float32, so model(features) would raise a dtype-mismatch RuntimeError at the first batch. CrossEntropyLoss also expects int64 class indices, so int32 or float labels would fail or be misinterpreted. nn.Linear(10, 3) also requires exactly 10 feature columns and labels in 0..2. Trigger: features.npz stores float64 or integer features (the NumPy default), non-int64 labels, a feature count other than 10, or more than 3 classes. Search boundary: no .float(), .long(), astype or dtype= anywhere in the notebook; features.npz is not in the workspace, so the actual dtypes and shapes are unresolved.
findings.suggestion: Use torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32) and torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.long), and build the layer as nn.Linear(X.shape[1], len(np.unique(y))).
findings.title: Tensor dtypes and hard-coded sizes likely make the first forward or loss call fail

findings.message: There is no epoch loop, so the model gets one Adam step per batch of 32, about 0.8*N/32 steps at lr=0.001. Unless the dataset is large, this is likely to leave the classifier undertrained, and the notebook reports nothing that would reveal it. Trigger: a dataset of modest size, where a few hundred or fewer small Adam steps do not converge. Search boundary: cell 3 is the only training code and has no outer loop.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the batch loop in for epoch in range(num_epochs): and track the loss per epoch.
findings.title: Training is a single pass over the data

findings.message: The test split is created but never used, the per-batch loss is never printed or stored, and the model is not saved. After running the notebook there is no way to tell whether the classifier learned anything, and the weights disappear with the kernel. Search boundary: all four cells; there is no print, logging, metric, torch.save, or use of X_test/y_test.
findings.suggestion: Add an evaluation cell: model.eval(), then under torch.no_grad() compute accuracy on X_test/y_test. Log the average loss during training and torch.save(model.state_dict(), ...) if the model is needed later.
findings.title: Nothing is evaluated, logged or saved

findings.message: Only train_test_split is seeded. The Linear initialisation and the DataLoader shuffle order use torch's unseeded RNG, so each run trains differently. Separately, the notebook's saved metadata has execution counts 1, 3, 2, 4 for cells 0-3: in the recorded session the scaling/split cell (count 2) ran before the loading cell (count 3), so it used an X left over from earlier kernel state. That is history, not proof of the current state, but it means the saved session was not a clean top-to-bottom run.
findings.suggestion: Call torch.manual_seed(...) (and np.random.seed if needed) in the first cell, then restart the kernel and run all cells in order before saving.
findings.title: Unseeded training, and recorded execution order differs from cell order

findings.message: Cell 0 imports from sklearn before cell 1 installs it. If scikit-learn is missing, cell 0 fails first and the install never helps. If it is present, the install is redundant work on every run and can change the environment mid-session. %matplotlib inline enables a backend that the notebook never uses.
findings.suggestion: Move dependency installation into a requirements file or the first cell, and remove the unused %matplotlib magic.
findings.title: !pip install scikit-learn runs after sklearn is imported
